name: Wool Crochet
basis: why: cloth built one loop at a time with a hook, rows worked in opposite directions; how: V stitches, alternating rows, shell border

lumenary.blurb: A crocheted blanket: the picture worked in rows of chunky stitches, each a small knot of two strands with its own highlight, in a handful of wool colours and with a shell border.

why: Crochet builds cloth one loop at a time with a single hook, and every stitch shows. A picture in crochet is a grid, like knitting, but the stitches are chunkier, each row is worked in the opposite direction to the last, and the edge is usually finished with a decorative border. The charm is in the slight unevenness of something made by hand.
how: Average the picture to one colour per stitch.
Find a few wool colours and give each stitch the nearest one.
Draw each stitch as two strands leaning into a V, each with a shadow and a highlight.
Shift every second row by half a stitch and reverse the overlap of its strands.
Work a border of shells, five stitches fanned from one foot.
Add a little fuzz: fine noise and the odd stray fibre.
history: Crochet as we know it appears in Europe in the early nineteenth century; the Dutch magazine Penélopé printed patterns in 1823. In Ireland during the famine of the 1840s, crocheted lace became a cottage industry that fed families. The granny square, made from leftover yarn, spread in the twentieth century, and Japan’s amigurumi, small crocheted creatures, made the craft popular with a new generation.
terms: The basic short stitch, worked into the row below.
Several stitches worked into one foot so that they fan out.
Reducing many colours to a small fixed set.
paragraphs: The picture is averaged down to one colour for each stitch, and a small palette of wools is found on that tiny image by k-means. Every stitch then takes the wool nearest to its own colour. Wool is matt, so the palette loses a little saturation and its lightness is squeezed away from pure black and white. When a basket of fixed colours is chosen instead, each palette colour is given a different colour from the basket, matched by its rank from dark to light and then by hue, so the picture keeps its tonal order.

One stitch is two strands of yarn leaning together into a V. Each strand is drawn three times along the same line: wide and dark, then narrower in the wool’s colour, then a thin light line off to one side. Together they read as a round thread lit from the left. Rows are worked back and forth, so every second row sits half a stitch across and its strands overlap the other way round. The shell border is the same stitch repeated five times around a shared foot, fanned by a fixed angle. Fuzz is a little noise and the occasional bright fibre over the whole piece.

Baby pastels redraw the picture in a soft basket of wools.
Many stitches without the border keep the most detail.
